SP omitted the first two memorized items, reversed the order of the remaining ones and reached for the Check List before any critical action had been taken. IP had to stop the exercise, state the sequence and take the aircraft while SP recovered the procedure from the publication.

SP produced the correct steps only after IP prompted each item verbally, and the sequence was completed roughly twenty seconds after the malfunction was announced. Recall reached the lower limit of the standard solely through verbal prompting by IP.

texts.0: SP, due to a fixation on regaining the planned track after the simulated malfunction, did not observe the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual. SP accelerated past the limit applicable to the assumed configuration and held it there while working the procedure, and did not identify the exceedance when the indications showed it. IP had to intervene on the controls to bring the aircraft back inside the published limits.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the navigation solution rather than on the engine and airspeed indications, did not keep the aircraft inside the applicable limits during the procedure. Parameters were at the published limit and returned inside it only after IP stated the limit and directed the correction. SP knew the figure when asked but had not been monitoring against it.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged after the descent was initiated, allowed the airspeed to increase toward the limit applicable to the condition. SP detected the trend on the cross-check, reduced power and stabilized the aircraft well inside the published limit without IP intervention. The remainder of the procedure was flown with the parameters controlled.
texts.3: SP knew and observed the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual throughout the handling of the emergency. Airspeed, power and configuration were kept inside the applicable figures while the procedure was executed and the recovery was planned. No limit was approached without a deliberate correction.
texts.4: SP handled the emergency entirely inside the Section V limits, quoting the applicable figure for the condition before setting the parameters and holding the aircraft comfortably clear of every boundary. SP also identified the limit that the intended descent profile would have challenged and adjusted the profile in advance. Deviations from the published limits were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP observed the Flight Manual limits within standards, but the airspeed was flown close to the applicable limit for a large part of the procedure and left no margin for a further change of configuration. The trend is toward operating on the boundary rather than inside it, which removes the buffer an actual emergency requires. SP is expected to select parameters with a deliberate margin below the published limits on the next sortie.

SP continued on the last heading with no time check, no climb for radio and radar coverage and no attempt to use the available navigation aids or to request assistance. IP had to take the aircraft, establish the position and direct the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position after two consecutive turning points were not identified, did not initiate the lost procedures without prompting. SP maintained heading and continued the search of the chart, and began the climb, the aid tuning and the request for assistance only after IP prompted each action in turn. The procedure was brought to the lower limit of the standard by that prompting, and several minutes of fuel were consumed before the position was fixed.
texts.2: SP, due to a turning point misidentified against a similar ground feature, initially continued on a track that did not match the planned leg. SP recognized within about a minute that position could not be confirmed, noted the time, climbed for coverage, tuned the available aid and re-established the position without IP intervention. The sortie continued on the planned route with the fuel plan intact.

SP noted the time and the last known position, held a suitable heading, climbed as required for radio and radar coverage, used the available navigation aids and requested assistance at the correct point. The position was re-established quickly and the recovery was planned with the fuel available.
texts.4: SP recognized at once that position could no longer be confirmed and executed the lost procedures with exceptional order, fixing the last known position and time, climbing for coverage, cross-checking two independent aids and stating the fuel available and the recovery options before requesting any assistance. The position was resolved with no loss of the planned timing. Deviations from the ideal procedure were negligible.

The trend is toward accepting uncertainty for longer than the fuel state or the weather would allow. error_modes.label: DIVERSION DECISION AND SELECTION OF A SUITABLE AIRFIELD WITH THE AVAILABLE FUEL

texts.0: SP, due to the alternate airfields not having been extracted from the planning material before the sortie, did not handle the emergency effectively in the diversion phase. SP had no distance, heading or fuel requirement available for any alternate and elected to continue toward the planned destination past the point where the fuel remaining supported it. IP had to select the diversion field, compute the requirement and direct the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to fuel figures for the alternates being carried only as rough estimates, did not decide the diversion in time. SP recognized the need to divert but produced a field selection and a fuel computation only after IP asked for the remaining fuel and the distance to each option. The decision reached the lower limit of the standard through that prompting and the aircraft landed with a reduced margin over the minimum.
texts.2: SP, due to a first selection based on distance alone, initially chose an alternate whose runway and approach did not suit the aircraft condition. SP reconsidered against the field data carried on the kneeboard, changed to a suitable airfield and recomputed the fuel required, all without IP intervention. The revised diversion was flown with the planned reserve preserved.
texts.3: SP handled the emergency effectively in the diversion phase, selecting a suitable airfield for the aircraft condition and computing heading, distance, time and fuel required against the fuel remaining. The decision was made at a point that preserved the reserve and the diversion was flown as computed. No element of the selection required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP identified the need to divert immediately, selected the most suitable airfield for the aircraft condition and the weather, and presented heading, distance, time, fuel required and expected reserve in a single organized statement. SP had already refreshed the alternate data at each turning point, so the figures needed no computation under pressure. Deviations from the optimum diversion solution were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP selected a suitable diversion field within standards, but the fuel computation was made once and never revised as the situation developed, and the reserve at the estimated landing time was only just above the minimum. The trend is toward a diversion plan that is correct at the moment it is made and stale thereafter. SP is expected to update the alternate figures at each turning point so the diversion decision rests on current fuel and distance data.

error_modes.label: DECLARATION OF THE EMERGENCY AND COORDINATION WITH ATC AND IP

texts.0: SP, due to a technically worded transmission where plain language was required to convey the emergency, did not declare the situation to ATC or state the aircraft condition to IP. The transmission described a system indication with no distress prefix, no intentions, no fuel and no souls on board, and the controller continued to handle the aircraft as routine traffic. IP had to take the radios, declare the emergency and obtain the priority handling required.
texts.1: SP, due to jargon that obscured the aircraft's actual condition, did not make the required declaration in a form ATC could act on. SP transmitted the malfunction by its cockpit indication and stated intentions only after IP directed the format and content of the call. The coordination reached the lower limit of the standard through that direction, and the priority handling was delayed by about a minute.
texts.2: SP, due to a first call that stated the problem without the intentions and the fuel remaining, did not give ATC a complete picture at the first transmission. SP recognized the omission, made a second call in plain language with condition, intentions, fuel and persons on board, and confirmed the clearance received, without IP intervention. The coordination was complete before the diversion turn was started.
texts.3: SP declared the emergency to ATC in plain language, stating the aircraft condition, intentions, fuel remaining and persons on board, and obtained the handling required. SP kept IP informed of the assessment and the intended course of action at each step. No transmission required correction or repetition.
texts.4: SP declared the emergency in a single clear transmission that gave ATC everything needed to act, kept subsequent calls short and unambiguous, and maintained a running plain-language assessment with IP so that both cockpits held the same picture. SP also confirmed the assistance available at the diversion field before it was offered. Deviations from standard emergency phraseology were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP declared the emergency and coordinated within standards, but the calls carried more system detail than ATC required and the intentions were stated last, so the controller had to ask for them. The trend is toward transmissions that describe the malfunction rather than the assistance needed. SP is expected to lead with condition and intentions in plain language on the next sortie.

texts_at.2: SP declared the emergency and coordinated with ATC and IP inside the standard required at this stage, a first call stating the problem without intentions and fuel remaining before a complete second call was made. texts_at.3: SP declared the emergency to ATC in plain language, stating the aircraft condition, intentions, fuel remaining and persons on board, and kept IP informed of the assessment at each step, the small margin tracing to one update to IP being given a beat after the assessment rather than with it. error_modes.label: SYSTEMS KNOWLEDGE AND SELECTION OF THE CORRECT PROCEDURE FOR THE CONDITION

texts.0: SP, due to the daily assignment on the affected system not having been prepared, did not know the emergency procedure or the system in detail and selected a procedure that did not apply to the indications presented. SP could not explain what the indication meant, what the system had done or what the procedure was intended to achieve, and persisted with the wrong procedure after it produced no change. IP had to identify the condition and direct the correct procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the system logic set as daily assignment, did not identify the condition from the indications without help. SP named two candidate procedures and selected the correct one only after IP pointed out the distinguishing indication. Knowledge was demonstrated at the lower limit of the standard and the questioning in the debrief showed the system operation was known only in outline.
texts.2: SP, due to two similar indications not having been separated during preparation, initially started the procedure for the adjacent condition. SP compared the remaining indications against the expected picture, recognized the mismatch and changed to the correct procedure without IP intervention. SP then explained the system operation and the reason for each step accurately.
texts.3: SP knew in detail the emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as daily assignment, identified the condition correctly from the indications presented and selected the applicable procedure without hesitation. SP explained the purpose of each step and the system behaviour behind it when questioned. No part of the identification required assistance from IP.
texts.4: SP identified the condition immediately, selected the correct procedure and explained the system logic, the reason for each step and the consequences of the failure for the remainder of the navigation profile. SP also described how the indications would differ for the adjacent conditions that could be confused with it. Deviations from complete systems knowledge were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP demonstrated the required systems knowledge within standards, but the identification of the condition rested on recognizing a familiar indication pattern rather than on understanding the system logic, and the explanation broke down when the questioning moved past the memorized steps. The trend is toward knowledge that will not transfer to a condition presented in an unfamiliar form. SP is expected to prepare the system operation, not only the procedure text, for the next daily assignment.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the condition from the indications and the applicable procedure, SP followed the selection read back and needed the condition named on two occasions during the sortie. texts_at.3: SP knew in detail the emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as daily assignment, identified the condition correctly from the indications presented and selected the applicable procedure without hesitation, the small margin tracing to one explanation of a step being given a beat slower than the rest when questioned. error_modes.label: CLIMB TO COPE AS THE FIRST REACTION TO AN EMERGENCY ON THE LOW LEVEL ROUTE
error_modes.source: technique:8.20.1 ABNORMAL PROCEDURES - EMERGENCIES (CLIMB TO COPE)

texts.0: SP, due to remaining at route altitude in order to keep the ground track in sight, did not climb to cope when the malfunction appeared on the low level leg. The analysis was attempted at low altitude with terrain filling the crosscheck, no altitude was traded for thinking time and the aircraft was still below the ridge line ahead when the procedure stalled. IP had to take the aircraft, initiate the climb and re-establish safe altitude before the situation could be analyzed.
texts.1: SP, due to treating the climb as a later step rather than as the first reaction, held route altitude while the indications were being read. The climb to cope was started about thirty seconds after the malfunction and only after IP directed it, and the height gained was the minimum that allowed the analysis rather than what the terrain and the problem required. The sequence was completed at the lower limit of the standard and with verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial attempt to diagnose the problem at route altitude, began the analysis before any altitude had been gained. SP recognized this within a few seconds, set climb power, traded the low level airspeed for altitude and completed the analysis well above the terrain, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP climbed to cope as the first reaction to the malfunction encountered on the route, without IP intervention. The climb was continued as high as necessary to analyze the situation safely, terrain clearance was assured before attention moved to the indications, and the analysis was then completed in an unhurried sequence.
texts.4: SP initiated the climb at the first indication of the malfunction, stated the intention to climb to cope and levelled only when the altitude gained gave clear terrain margin and radio coverage for the analysis. The problem was then worked with the aircraft trimmed and stable and the route position was preserved throughout. Deviations from the technique were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP climbed to cope on each occasion and analyzed the problem above the terrain, but the climb was stopped at the first altitude that felt comfortable rather than at the altitude the situation required. The trend is to preserve the low level picture at the cost of the margin that makes an unhurried analysis possible. SP is expected to state a target altitude for the climb and to continue to it before starting the analysis.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the climb to begin before any analysis, SP followed the climb on the controls after the call on two of the malfunctions introduced. Climbing to cope as the first reaction without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin one climb unprompted before doing so for every malfunction.
texts_at.1: SP climbed to cope as the first reaction to the malfunction inside the standard required at this stage, the climb started about thirty seconds after the malfunction and only after IP directed it. texts_at.2: SP climbed to cope as the first reaction to the malfunction inside the standard required at this stage, an initial attempt to diagnose the problem begun at route altitude before the climb was recognized as the priority within a few seconds. texts_at.3: SP climbed to cope as the first reaction to the malfunction encountered on the route, without IP intervention, continuing as high as necessary to analyze the situation safely, terrain clearance assured before attention moved to the indications, the small margin tracing to the target altitude being decided a beat after the climb started rather than before it. texts_above.3: SP climbed to cope as the first reaction to the malfunction encountered on the route, without IP intervention, the climb continued as high as necessary to analyze the situation safely, terrain clearance assured before attention moved to the indications. error_modes.label: ENGINE FAILURE AT LOW LEVEL - WINGTIP ARC TURN, ZOOM RESTART AND EJECTION DECISION
error_modes.source: technique:8.20.2 ENGINE MALFUNCTIONS AT LOW LEVEL

texts.0: SP, due to working the restart before turning, did not make an immediate turn and climb toward an airfield inside the arc circumscribed by the wingtips when the engine failed on the route. The zoom was flown straight ahead away from the only field within approximately 3 miles, no N1 rise was checked at the apex and the ejection decision was never addressed while air starts were attempted below 2000 feet AGL. IP had to take the aircraft, turn toward the field and direct the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitating over which field to use, delayed the turn and climb until IP called the field inside the wingtip arc. The zoom was then flown, but the check for an N1 rise by the apex and the ejection decision were both made only after prompting, and the aircraft arrived over the field with the glide profile at its minimum. The response met the lower limit of the standard with verbal direction at each step.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial turn toward a larger field outside engine-out range, started the recovery on a track that the energy available did not support. SP re-evaluated within about ten seconds, turned to the field inside the arc circumscribed by the wingtips, converted the route airspeed into approximately 1000 feet of zoom altitude and checked for an N1 rise at the apex, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP made an immediate turn and climb in the direction of a suitable field inside the arc circumscribed by the wingtips, without IP intervention. The restart was considered within the zoom, the indications were checked for an N1 rise by the apex and the criterion for ejecting was stated and honoured. No air start was attempted below 2000 feet AGL.
texts.4: SP turned and climbed toward the field inside the wingtip arc at the first indication of engine failure, naming the field and its distance from the pre-mission map study. The zoom was flown to convert route energy into altitude, the restart was attempted within it and the absence of an N1 rise by the apex was called at once together with the ejection decision. Nothing was traded for an air start below 2000 feet AGL and the glide profile stayed inside the planned margin.
texts.marginal: SP turned and climbed toward the field inside the wingtip arc and flew the zoom correctly, but the ejection criterion was stated only when IP asked what would follow if the engine did not relight. The tendency is to treat the restart as the whole plan and to leave the ejection decision until the altitude has already been spent. SP is expected to state the ejection gate before the zoom is started on the next low level sortie.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the field inside the wingtip arc and the checks for the zoom and restart, SP followed the turn on the controls after the call. Turning toward a field inside the wingtip arc without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP at this stage. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to turn toward the arc unprompted on one occasion before doing so for every engine failure introduced.
texts_at.1: SP handled the engine failure at low level inside the standard required at this stage, the turn and climb toward the field inside the wingtip arc flown only after IP called the field. The trend traces to hesitation over which field to use rather than an immediate turn toward the arc circumscribed by the wingtips. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to turn toward the wingtip arc immediately, before selecting between fields, so the turn does not need to be called.
texts_at.2: SP handled the engine failure at low level inside the standard required at this stage, an initial turn made toward a larger field outside engine-out range before the track was re-evaluated within about ten seconds. texts_at.3: SP made an immediate turn and climb in the direction of a suitable field inside the arc circumscribed by the wingtips, without IP intervention, the restart considered within the zoom and the ejection criterion stated and honoured, the small margin tracing to the N1 check at the apex being made a beat after the apex rather than at it. error_modes.label: ROUTE ABORT INTO IMC - IMMEDIATE CLIMB TO THE ERAA AND SQUAWK 7700
error_modes.source: technique:8.20.3 MINIMUM SAFE ALTITUDE (MSA), EMERGENCY ROUTE ABORT ALTITUDE (ERAA) AND ROUTE ABORTS

texts.0: SP, due to treating the entry into cloud as a weather deviation rather than as an emergency, did not execute an immediate climb to the emergency route abort altitude and did not squawk 7700. The aircraft was manoeuvred in IMC below the highest MSA of the planned legs, no controlling agency was contacted and the terrain along the abort track was never considered. IP had to take the aircraft, climb to the ERAA and obtain a clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation over which altitude applied, began the abort climb toward the MSA of the current leg instead of the ERAA and had to be corrected. The 7700 code was selected about forty seconds after the abort was initiated and the call to ATC was made only after IP directed it. The abort was eventually flown correctly but at the lower limit of the standard and with prompting at each step.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial reaction of turning back toward the last area of good visibility, delayed the climb by a few seconds after entering IMC. SP then declared the abort, climbed immediately to the ERAA, squawked 7700 and contacted the controlling agency while flying a proper VFR altitude until a clearance was received, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP treated the abort into IMC as an emergency, executing an immediate climb to the emergency route abort altitude as a minimum and squawking 7700. Contact with the appropriate ATC agency was established and the proper VFR altitude was flown until an IFR clearance was received. No element of the abort required correction by IP.
texts.4: SP recognized the abort criteria before the route entered the deteriorating weather and stated the ERAA and the abort track in advance. The climb was initiated at once, 7700 was selected without prompting, the controlling agency received position and intentions, and terrain clearance was assured against the highest MSA of the legs throughout. The abort was completed with negligible deviation from the planned track and altitude.
texts.marginal: SP aborted the route to the ERAA and squawked 7700 within standards, but the decision to abort was taken after the visibility had already forced two heading changes off the planned leg. The trend is to keep working the route in deteriorating conditions instead of applying the abort criteria when they are met. SP is expected to set a weather abort decision point during the brief and to honour it in flight.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the climb to the ERAA and the 7700 squawk, SP followed the climb and the transponder selection after the call. Executing the immediate climb and squawk without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin the climb unprompted on one abort before doing so for every abort.
texts_at.1: SP applied the route abort into IMC inside the standard required at this stage, the 7700 code selected about forty seconds after the abort was initiated and the ATC call made only after IP directed it. SP is expected to climb to the ERAA immediately on the abort, without weighing which altitude applies, so 7700 follows without delay.

error_modes.label: ANXIETY DISORIENTATION AND WANDERING AIMLESSLY WHILE PLANNING WHAT TO DO NEXT

texts.0: SP, due to anxiety disorientation after the chart to ground method failed to identify an anticipated landmark, concluded that the aircraft was lost while it was in fact on course. SP abandoned the pre-planned headings and times and wandered on random headings while deciding what to do, so the last known position was lost, no clock time was written down and the fuel state was never checked against the minimum fuel required. IP had to stop the manoeuvring, re-establish the position from the log and restore the route.
texts.1: SP, due to anxiety disorientation over a single unidentified feature, began to alter heading in search of a recognizable landmark instead of holding a temporary plan. The time was noted and the pre-planned heading resumed only after IP directed both actions, some two minutes after the doubt arose, and the extent of the error then had to be reconstructed from the log. The situation was contained at the lower limit of the standard and with verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an anticipated landmark not appearing at the computed time, briefly doubted the position and started a turn off the planned leg. SP recognized the reaction as anxiety disorientation within about fifteen seconds, wrote down the clock time, resumed the pre-planned heading and time and identified the following feature as planned, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP did not complicate the situation when an expected landmark failed to appear, keeping a cool head and allowing for anxiety disorientation. SP checked the clock immediately and wrote down the time, decided on the temporary plan of continuing the pre-planned headings and times, and checked the fuel state against the minimum fuel required. No aimless manoeuvring occurred and IP made no calls.
texts.4: SP treated the missing landmark as a chart to ground problem rather than as proof of being lost, noting the clock time at once and reviewing progress from the last known position. The pre-planned heading and time were held while the possible causes of heading, airspeed, timing and wind error were reviewed, the fuel state was compared with the minimum fuel required and a charted known landmark was nominated for the next check. Position was confirmed without a single heading change off the planned leg.
texts.marginal: SP held the pre-planned heading and time when the expected feature failed to appear and avoided wandering while planning what to do next, but the clock time was written down only at the second moment of doubt. The trend is to spend the first moments searching the chart before starting the timing record that later fixes the extent of any error. SP is expected to check the clock immediately, before any further map study, whenever position becomes doubtful.

error_modes.label: EMERGENCY AIRFIELDS AND 10 NM DIVERSION LINES ANNOTATED IN PLANNING
error_modes.source: technique:8.18.3.m-n AIRSPACE ANNOTATION AND EMERGENCY AIRFIELDS (DIVERSION LINES)

texts.0: SP, due to the map study for potential emergency diverts being omitted before the mission, had no emergency airfield associated with the leg being flown when the malfunction occurred. The chart carried no emergency airfields in red and no diversion lines, so the nearest field, its heading and its distance had to be searched for while the aircraft continued away from it. IP had to nominate the field and direct the diversion.
texts.1: SP, due to emergency airfields having been annotated only around the departure and the destination, could not name the divert field for the middle legs of the route. Heading and distance were derived in flight after IP asked for them, about a minute after the problem arose, and the diversion line that would have given both was missing from the chart. The requirement was met at its lower limit and only with prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to two emergency airfields having been annotated without diversion lines, initially estimated heading and distance by eye off the chart. SP recognized the imprecision at once, used the plotted route and the turning point positions to derive heading and distance to the nearer field and started the diversion on the correct track, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP had selected suitable airfields along the planned route as possible emergency landing areas during planning, joining the two closest suitable fields and using the bisector to define the emergency airfield for each portion of the route. Diversion lines of 10 nm were drawn and the emergency airfields were depicted in red, so field, heading and distance were available immediately when they were needed. No element required completion by IP.
texts.4: SP annotated the chart with airspace, hazard areas and emergency airfields in red before the sortie, applying the bisector between the two closest suitable fields and drawing 10 nm diversion lines for each leg. When the malfunction occurred, SP named the applicable emergency airfield, its heading and its distance from the annotated chart alone, and the fuel required was already known from planning. The diversion was started with no delay for chart work.
texts.marginal: SP annotated emergency airfields and diversion lines for the whole route, but the bisector was applied loosely on two legs, so the field nominated in flight was not the nearest suitable one. The trend is to complete the annotation as a chart formality rather than as the source of the divert decision. SP is expected to verify each bisector against the plotted route before the chart is accepted as complete.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the emergency airfield and its heading and distance from the annotated chart, SP followed the divert read back and needed the field named before two turning points on the route. Naming an emergency airfield from the annotated chart without a reminder has not yet been asked of SP independently. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to name one emergency airfield unprompted before doing so for every leg.

error_modes.label: SINGLE-ENGINE MENTALITY - USEABLE TORQUE, FIRE FOD OR FROZEN, AND MINIMUM EJECTION ALTITUDE

texts.0: SP, due to running the shutdown items on an engine that was still producing useable torque, secured a powerplant that was not confirmed on fire, was not vibrating with indications of impending failure and was still required for the recovery. The restart criteria of fire, FOD or frozen were never assessed and no minimum ejection altitude had been set, so the aircraft was committed to a glide it could not complete. IP had to take the aircraft and manage the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete assessment of the fire, FOD or frozen criteria, could not state whether a restart should be attempted until IP asked for each criterion in turn. The minimum ejection altitude was set about a minute into the recovery and after prompting, and the glide distance was computed without the elevation of the field. The decisions were reached at the lower limit of the standard and with verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to the field elevation being omitted from the first glide calculation, initially assessed the airfield as being within range when it was marginal. SP rechecked within about twenty seconds, included the field elevation and the intervening terrain along the route of flight, revised the plan to the nearer field and set a minimum ejection altitude, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP applied single-engine mentality throughout, keeping the engine running while it produced useable torque and assessing the restart question against fire, FOD or frozen. Glide distance was computed with field elevation included and with the intervening terrain considered, and a minimum ejection altitude was set once immediate ejection was not warranted. Awareness of the nearest suitable emergency airfields was maintained without IP intervention.
texts.4: SP maintained awareness of the nearest suitable emergency airfields on every leg and responded to the unusual engine indications by recovering to a suitable field. The engine was left running while it produced useable torque, the restart question was answered against fire, FOD or frozen, glide distance was computed with field elevation and intervening terrain, and a minimum ejection altitude was set with update points nominated to assess the profile. SP stated the point at which recovery would be abandoned in favour of ejection.

The trend is to treat ejection as the outcome of a failed glide rather than as a decision made in advance. error_modes.label: EMERGENCY ON THE FORMATION NAVIGATION SORTIE - NUMBER 1 POSITION AND ROUTE SPACING

texts.0: SP, due to attempting to hold fingertip position while working the malfunction on the formation navigation sortie, did not increase separation and did not accept the Number 1 position when it was offered. The aircraft was flown closer than route spacing in VMC with the problem unresolved, no Knock It Off was called and Number 1 was never told the nature of the problem or the assistance required. IP had to call Knock It Off, obtain the separation and take over the handling of the emergency.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to change formation position while a checklist was open, remained as Number 2 with the malfunction until IP directed the acceptance of the lead. Number 1 was informed of the problem about a minute late and only after prompting, and the intentions and the assistance required were never volunteered. The formation was managed at the lower limit of the standard and with verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial decision to stay in position until the checklist was complete, held fingertip spacing for a short period after the malfunction appeared. SP recognized the workload this created, called Knock It Off, moved out to route, informed Number 1 of the problem and the intentions, and took the Number 1 position when it was next offered, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP called Knock It Off on encountering the malfunction, informed Number 1 of the problem, the intentions and the assistance required, and increased separation before handling the emergency. The Number 1 position was taken when offered, SP being able to communicate and navigate, and the formation stayed no closer than route spacing thereafter. No element required direction by IP.
texts.4: SP called Knock It Off immediately, stated the malfunction, the intentions and the assistance required, and moved out of fingertip before any checklist was opened. The Number 1 position was accepted at the first offer and the recovery was led back to a straight in, while the other aircraft was used to report the conditions at the intended runway. Formation integrity and mutual support were preserved for the whole recovery.
texts.marginal: SP took the Number 1 position and increased separation to route, but the offer had to be repeated before it was accepted and the assistance required was stated only in general terms. The trend is to treat the change of position as a loss of the mission rather than as the means of freeing capacity for the emergency. SP is expected to accept the lead at the first offer and to state precisely what the other aircraft is to do.

error_modes.label: LOST WINGMAN PROCEDURE IN IMC - 15 DEGREES OF BANK FOR 15 SECONDS AND SMOOTH INPUTS

texts.0: SP, due to continuing to search for Number 1 after the formation entered cloud on the route, did not execute the lost wingman procedure when visual contact was lost. No turn away was made, no transition to instruments was started and the aircraft was held on the last known relative position with Number 1 uninformed and no separate clearance requested. IP had to take the aircraft, obtain separation and request the clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to delaying the decision until the visual references were completely gone, executed the turn away roughly ten seconds after visual contact was lost and only after IP directed it. The 15 degrees of bank was held for less than the required 15 seconds and Number 1 was informed after the fact, so the separation obtained was at the lower limit of what the procedure is meant to provide.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial hesitation over which lost wingman case applied while inside the turn, started with the wings-level procedure. SP corrected within a few seconds, momentarily reduced power for nose-tail separation, told Number 1 to roll out and maintained the angle of bank for lateral separation before obtaining a separate clearance, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP executed the applicable lost wingman procedure as soon as visual contact was lost, transitioning to instruments simultaneously. The turn away was flown with 15 degrees of bank for 15 seconds, Number 1 was informed, course was resumed and a separate clearance was obtained without IP intervention.
texts.4: SP transitioned to instruments and executed the correct lost wingman case at the moment visual contact was lost, using smooth control inputs that kept the effects of spatial disorientation to a minimum. The 15 degrees of bank was held for the full 15 seconds, the call to Number 1 was made without delay and the separate clearance was requested and read back while the aircraft stayed within 100 feet of the assigned altitude. Terrain and obstacles along the flight path were considered rather than assumed to be cleared by the procedure.
texts.marginal: SP executed the correct lost wingman procedure and obtained a separate clearance, but the control inputs at the start of the turn away were firmer than the technique requires and the instrument crosscheck lagged for the first seconds. The trend is toward abrupt inputs at the moment of losing sight, which aggravates spatial disorientation exactly when the transition to instruments is being made. SP is expected to apply the bank smoothly and to establish the crosscheck before the turn is complete.
